nate-bittle: Toronto got a skilled seven-footer who blocked 2.8 shots a game in Vegas while pulling down nearly seven boards in only 20 minutes. Bittle's Oregon tape was always about touch and timing rather than brute force, and the per-minute rim protection is legit. He needs weight to hold up against NBA centers over 82 games. Deep-league big-man asset with real category juice if the minutes come.
jaron-pierre-jr: Pierre put up 10 a game in limited Vegas run for a Pelicans team that badly needs perimeter shooting. He's a straight-line scorer who gets to his spots, though three games is too small a sample to draw much beyond "he can fill it up." Playmaking and defense are the swing skills. Watchlist asset in deeper formats.
trey-kaufman-renn: Kaufman-Renn was one of college basketball's most efficient interior scorers at Purdue, but Minnesota gave him only 12 minutes a night in Vegas and the production followed. That's his projection in a sentence: polished post skill in a league that keeps shrinking the post. If he stretches his range he sticks. Low-priority asset until the role clarifies.
quadir-copeland: Copeland was one of the most disruptive guards in Vegas, averaging 2.6 steals in 29 minutes while running Houston's second unit for 13 a night. He's a huge lead guard who bothers passing lanes and gets downhill whenever he wants. The jumper is the thing standing between him and real minutes. In steals-heavy category leagues he's a sneaky asset.
vsevolod-ishchenko: Ishchenko filled the box score modestly across the board for Dallas — 9.6 points, 4.4 boards, 3 assists in nearly 28 minutes. That's the profile: a connective wing who does several things without dominating any of them. Those players either become rotation glue or wash out on shooting percentage. Watch the three-point rate.
tobi-lawal: Lawal is an energy four whose Vegas line, under six points in 19 minutes, reflects a game built on effort plays rather than shot creation. He rebounds, defends, and finishes what's created for him. That archetype needs either elite athleticism or a jumper to stick around. Deep stash only.
tyler-nickel: Nickel got real run for the Knicks in Vegas, nearly 29 minutes a night, and rewarded it with 12 a game. He's a shooter first, which is the most portable skill in the league, and New York has always found minutes for wings who space the floor. Defense is the open question. Worth a late roster spot in deeper dynasty formats.
tyler-bilodeau: Bilodeau's Vegas numbers were quiet, but Brooklyn is about the best landing spot a young big could ask for simply because nobody is blocking the runway. He's a skilled scoring four who has to prove he can defend NBA fives. Patience asset on a team that will give him rope.
felix-okpara: Okpara is exactly what he was in college: a rim-running, shot-blocking center who scores off other people's creation. Eight points, 5.5 boards and better than a block in 22 Vegas minutes is a fair representation. Washington's frontcourt is unsettled enough that he could steal minutes. Rebounds-and-blocks specialist asset.
lajae-jones: Jones played more Vegas games than any other Warrior and put up a steady 8.7 in 16 minutes a night. Golden State's system rewards wings who move without the ball and make quick decisions, which suits him. He'll need to shoot a high clip to climb that depth chart. Long-shot asset in an excellent development org.
jack-kayil: Kayil ran point for the Knicks' summer squad and posted a clean 3.5 assists with 1.8 steals in 22 minutes. He plays with pace and pressures the ball, which is how young guards earn trust. The scoring efficiency needs work before he's more than a third guard. Depth asset.
bryce-hopkins: Hopkins was one of the best players in Vegas, going for 18 and 6.5 in 26 minutes for Denver. Before injuries derailed his Providence career he was a legitimate high-major star, and the skill never left — he scores from all three levels and rebounds his position. If the knee holds, he's the best value in this tier of the draft. That's a real if, and the price reflects it.
nick-martinelli: Martinelli scored 14.8 a game in Vegas the same way he did at Northwestern: angles, footwork, and an unteachable feel for finishing over bigger defenders. He isn't an explosive athlete, which is why he lasted this long, and the Clippers will find out whether the craft translates against NBA length. Points-league managers should pay attention.
jaden-bradley: Bradley is a defense-first lead guard who ran Toronto's summer offense without forcing a thing — 3.2 assists, low usage, steady throughout. Arizona fans know the profile: he defends the point of attack and makes the simple play. The scoring has to come for him to be more than a third guard. Modest but real asset.
trevon-brazile: Brazile went for 18.7 and 8.3 across three Vegas games and looked every bit the athlete Arkansas fans remember before the ACL. He runs, jumps, blocks shots and stretches the floor, which is the entire modern-big starter kit. Health is the whole question with him. High-upside asset with an injury discount already baked in.
dillon-mitchell: Mitchell's 2.7 steals per game in Vegas is the number that jumps off the page — that's disruption you can't teach. He's an elite athlete who defends multiple positions and finishes above the rim. The jumper has never come around, and Boston will keep him only if the defense is genuinely special. Category-league asset for steals and percentages.
jakobi-gillespie: Gillespie put up 16 and 4.3 assists with two steals a night in Vegas, which is more or less exactly who he was in college: a productive, pesky lead guard who plays bigger than his frame. San Antonio's guard room is crowded, so the path is narrow. Deep-league asset who'll produce whenever the minutes appear.
izaiyah-nelson: Nelson barely played in Vegas and the line reflects it. He's a raw, athletic big in an Orlando system that has been patient with young frontcourt players before. There's nothing to project on yet — file the name rather than spend a roster spot. Revisit after his first G League stretch.
braden-smith: Seven assists a game in Vegas. Smith was the best passer in college basketball at Purdue and it translated immediately — he sees plays before they develop, and Indiana's pace-and-space system is a perfect stylistic match. The scoring and the size limitations are real and will cap his ceiling. In assist-heavy formats he's a legitimately valuable asset right now.
ugonna-onyenso: Onyenso is a specialist: 1.8 blocks in under 18 Vegas minutes with almost no offensive involvement. That's the entire scouting report at this stage — he protects the rim and does little else. Detroit can afford to develop him slowly. Blocks-only asset in deep category leagues.
emanuel-sharp: Sharp averaged 15.8 with 2.8 steals for Sacramento in Vegas, pairing the shooting he showed at Houston with real defensive activity. Kelvin Sampson guards tend to arrive with good habits and it shows. He's undersized for a two, so the handle and playmaking have to grow. Shooting-plus-steals asset worth a flier.
ryan-conwell: One game, 19 points. Conwell has been a high-volume shooter everywhere he's played, and Miami has the best track record in the league of turning exactly this profile into a rotation player. Tiny sample, obvious skill. If you believe in Heat development, he's the asset to bet on in this tier.
isaiah-evans: Evans is a pure wing shooter — 12.7 a game in Vegas on real minutes for Minnesota. At Duke he was the guy who could swing a game in three possessions and then go quiet for stretches. The frame needs weight and the defense needs work, but shooters with his release always get chances. Upside asset.
baba-miller: Miller's Vegas line, 12 points with 1.4 blocks, shows the tools that made him a recruiting prize: length, mobility, and enough skill to operate out to the arc. Consistency has never matched the flashes. The Clippers can be patient with him. Long-view asset with genuine physical upside.
henri-veesaar: Veesaar gives Atlanta a mobile modern center — 10 points and 1.4 blocks in 20 Vegas minutes, with the footwork you'd expect from someone developed in European systems. He needs strength to hold position against NBA bigs. Skilled-big asset in a league that keeps finding minutes for them.
alex-karaban: Karaban won two national titles at UConn being exactly what his Vegas line says he is: an 8-point, 4-rebound connective forward who never breaks the offense. Coaches love him, fantasy managers rarely do. He'll have a long career providing spacing and defense. Low-ceiling, high-floor asset.
meleek-thomas: Twenty-seven a game. Thomas was the leading scorer in Vegas by a wide margin and looked like a man among boys getting to his spots. The Arkansas freshman was always a bucket-getter and Cleveland just found one cheap. Efficiency and defense are the questions that come with that usage. If you buy one second-round asset from this class, make it this one.
joshua-jefferson: Two games and modest numbers, but two steals a night hints at the defensive instincts that made him productive at Iowa State. Brooklyn's roster is wide open, which helps. There isn't much to project on yet. Deep watchlist asset.
zuby-ejiofor: Ejiofor went for 12.5 and 5 in limited Vegas action, continuing the physical, motor-driven interior play he showed at St. John's. He's undersized for a five and not quite a stretch four, which is the whole projection question in one line. Atlanta will give him a look. Deep-league asset.
chris-cenac-jr: Cenac's Vegas line is the most exciting of any young big in this class: 10.5 points, 8 rebounds and 2.8 blocks in 23 minutes. He's long, mobile and genuinely modern, and Boston can develop him without any pressure. The frame needs filling out and the offensive role is undefined. Category-league asset with real upside.
bruce-thornton: Thornton played more minutes than any other Rocket in Vegas and produced across the board — 18.6 points, 4.4 assists, 2.6 steals. He was the steady heartbeat of Ohio State teams for three years and the pro game hasn't fazed him. He's undersized and not a burner, so the shooting has to hold up. Ready-now asset who could contribute before flashier rookies do.
koa-peat: Peat going home to Phoenix is a nice story and a sound basketball fit. He put up 16.8 a game in Vegas playing the same bruising, downhill style that made him one of the most decorated players Arizona has produced. The jumper and the defensive versatility are the swing skills. Solid mid-tier rookie asset with local juice.
tarris-reed-jr: Reed grabbed 8.7 boards a game in Vegas, which is simply what he does — a genuine rebounding specialist with soft hands around the rim. San Antonio's frontcourt is spoken for at the top, so this is a development play. Rebounding asset in deep category formats.
sergio-de-larrea: Nearly nine assists a game. De Larrea has been running pro offenses in Spain since he was a teenager and it shows — the pick-and-roll reads are years ahead of his age. Dallas got a genuine floor general. The scoring and the defense will be tested by NBA athletes. In assist formats he's one of the better long-term assets in this draft.
karim-lopez: One eleven-minute Vegas cameo with no points tells you essentially nothing. Lopez has been productive in the NBL against grown men, which is a far better indicator than a single summer game. Memphis has been good at developing this exact profile. Buy the résumé, not the box score.
labaron-philon: Philon led Philadelphia's summer squad in minutes and produced 18.5 points with 5.8 assists. He's a slippery downhill guard who creates for others once the defense collapses, and the Sixers need young guard depth badly. Strength and consistency are the development items. Strong second-tier asset with a clear path to minutes.
christian-anderson-jr: Anderson ran Charlotte's summer offense competently at 10.4 points and 4.2 assists, and Charlotte is about as open a depth chart as exists in the league. He's a scoring-minded guard who has to prove he can run a team full time. Modest asset, good situation.
dailyn-swain: Twenty-eight minutes a night and only 4.3 points — Swain's Vegas run was about everything except scoring. He's a long, versatile defender who rebounds and moves the ball, and that's a real NBA skill set. The jumper is the entire question. Defense-first asset for deep formats.
maliq-brown: Brown averaged 2.8 steals in Vegas, which is absurd for a forward and completely in character — he was one of the best team defenders in college basketball at Duke. He doesn't score, and that isn't changing quickly. In category leagues, steals from a big man is a genuinely rare asset.
tahaad-pettiford: Pettiford put up 15.4 a game at Auburn as one of the most fearless shot-makers in the SEC. He's a small guard who plays enormous, getting to his spots against anyone and hitting shots that have no business going in. Size and defense are what NBA teams will litigate. If the assist rate climbs this season, so does his stock.
xavier-booker: Booker's UCLA numbers, 7.3 and 3.5, still don't match the recruiting hype, and that gap is the whole story. The tools are obvious: a legitimate seven-footer who moves well and shoots it. The production has never followed. He's the definition of a buy-low asset, with the honest caveat that some prospects never convert tools into games.
solo-ball: Ball is a movement shooter in the UConn machine, which is about the best finishing school there is for the archetype. Nearly 13 a game with real efficiency. He'll have to show he can create off the dribble and defend NBA twos. Specialist asset whose value spikes if the percentages stay elite.
elliot-cadeau: Cadeau's 5.8 assists led a Michigan team that played through him constantly. He's a genuine table-setter with elite vision and pace who has always been young for his class. The jumper and the turnovers are the two things between him and the lottery. Assist-format asset with real upside if the shot arrives.
zvonimir-ivisic: A seven-foot-two center who blocks two shots a game and shoots threes is going to keep getting chances. Ivišić's counting stats are modest because the minutes were, but the per-minute rim protection is real. Strength and consistency are the issues. Category-league stash with blocks upside.
johann-grunloh: Grünloh blocked 2.2 shots a game in his first season at Virginia, which is the skill that travels fastest. He's a mobile European big with touch who's still adjusting to American physicality. Bigs like this often take a real leap in year two. Solid long-view asset.
pryce-sandfort: Sandfort scored 18.1 a game for Nebraska and has legitimate size for a wing shooter. The stroke is the calling card, and volume scorers who genuinely shoot it always find a floor. Defense and athleticism are the questions NBA teams will ask. Underrated asset in a deep class.
tomislav-ivisic: The more polished of the Ivišić brothers, Tomislav put up 10.4 and 5.6 with real passing feel from the center spot. He plays a modern, skilled brand of big-man basketball. He has to prove he can defend in space. Steady asset with a clearer NBA role than most college bigs.
cayden-boozer: The other Boozer twin is a completely different player from Cameron — a steady, high-feel point guard who ran Duke's offense without needing shots. His 7.7 and 3 assists undersell the connective value. He needs to score more to be drafted where the surname suggests. Interesting asset if you can separate the player from the name.
matas-vokietaitis: Vokietaitis put up 15.6 and 7.1 as a true interior scorer at Texas, which is increasingly rare and increasingly hard to project. He's productive, strong, and skilled with his back to the basket. Whether it translates comes down entirely to his mobility defending NBA pick-and-roll. Points-and-boards asset with real production behind it.
dame-sarr: Sarr's Duke numbers were quiet at 6.4 a game, but he's a big wing who played professionally in Europe before college and whose defensive tools show up beyond the box score. The offensive game has to catch up to the frame. Patience asset with an NBA body already in place.
rueben-chinyelu: An 11.2-rebound average is the headline — Chinyelu was one of the best rebounders in college basketball for a Florida team that won by controlling the glass. He finishes what's created and protects the rim. The offensive skill is largely limited to dunks and putbacks. Rebounding asset with a clearly defined role.
andrej-stojakovic: Stojaković scored 13.5 a game at Illinois with the pedigree and smooth mechanics you'd expect from the bloodline. He gets buckets in a variety of ways. Efficiency and defensive intensity are the gaps. Name-brand asset whose value hinges on the jumper falling at a pro clip.
alex-condon: Condon's line — 15.1 points, 7.5 rebounds, 3.6 assists — is the profile of a genuinely modern big. He passes, defends, rebounds and scores inside and out, and he did it for a top program. The Australian's stock has climbed steadily and deserves to. One of the safer non-lottery assets in this class.
trey-mckenney: McKenney played all 40 games as a freshman for Michigan and scored 9.9 in a supporting role. He's a physically mature wing scorer whose body is already NBA-ready. He needs to expand his game beyond mid-range scoring. Solid asset with room to grow into a bigger role.
tyler-tanner: Tanner's numbers are outstanding across the board — 19.5 points, 5.1 assists, 2.4 steals — and he's one of the more underrated producers in this class. He controls games at Vanderbilt on both ends. Level of competition and physical tools will get scrutinized. Statistical-darling asset worth grabbing before the boards catch up.
david-mirkovic: Mirković put up 13.3 and 8 with legitimate passing chops from the four spot. He's skilled, productive, and plays with a European feel for the game. Athleticism is the concern that keeps coming up. Well-rounded asset with a strong statistical foundation.
malachi-moreno: Moreno's freshman numbers at Kentucky were modest, but the shape is right: 6.3 boards and 1.5 blocks in a limited role. He's a big, physical center who defends the rim. Year-two production is what will actually move his stock. Patience asset.
alijah-arenas: Fourteen games, 14.1 points. Arenas's season was cut short, but the scoring instincts that made him a top recruit were clearly there. He's a shot creator with pedigree and a real handle. Health and efficiency are the open questions. High-variance asset whose price may never be lower than right now.
billy-richmond-iii: Richmond was a productive two-way wing for Arkansas at 11.2 and 4.3. He defends, cuts, competes, and his frame holds up against physical opponents. The jumper is the swing skill, as it always is for this archetype. Reasonable asset with a defined path.
motiejus-krivas: Krivas went for 10.4 and 8.2 with nearly two blocks a night, a genuine seven-foot rebounder and rim protector for a good Arizona team. He's mobile for his size and finishes well around the rim. Foul trouble and offensive polish are the development items. Traditional-big asset with strong per-game production.
ivan-kharchenkov: Kharchenkov fills every column a little — 10.4 points, 4.3 rebounds, 2.3 assists, 1.4 steals — as a big connective wing for Arizona. He has pro experience in Germany and plays a mature brand of basketball. He needs one standout skill to separate himself. Well-rounded asset.
patrick-ngongba-ii: Ngongba's 10.1 and 5.8 came with genuinely good passing for a center at Duke. He has soft hands, real touch, and enough size to anchor the five spot. Health and conditioning have been the historical concerns. Skilled-big asset with lottery-level flashes.
thomas-haugh: Haugh's 17.1 and 6.1 made him one of the most productive forwards in the SEC. He shoots it, moves it, and defends multiple spots — the connective four every NBA team is looking for. Athletic limitations are the knock. Production-based asset who tends to be underrated by tools-focused boards.
amari-allen: Allen contributed everywhere for Alabama — 11.4 points, 6.9 rebounds, 3.1 assists — as a big wing who rebounds and initiates offense. That versatility is exactly what modern rotations need. The shooting has to become reliable. Balanced asset with real statistical support.
davis-fogle: Fogle's 8.6 a game in a limited Gonzaga role undersells a shooter with genuine size. The Zags have a long track record of developing wings into pros across multiple seasons. He's a year-two breakout candidate. Cheap asset to hold before the production arrives.
